title: Are there any modern filmmakers like De Palma or Argento?

commenti.body:
Gasper Noe does a lot of spectacular shit with the camera.

Check out

- Irreversible (2002)
- Enter the Void (2009)

Wouldnt compare him to De Palma but maybe Argento… and Argento stars in his film Vortex (2021).

I would like to say though that it’s quite possible that you know all of this already.

I just want to point out that it is damn near irresponsible to recommend Irreversible without the disclaimer that this movie is beyond tough to watch and features one of the most intense brutal scenes ever filmed. Do not just throw this on the way you would a De Palma or Argento film.
OK Mary Whitehouse, noted. 🫡
Ur fine with the rape scene in Stendhal Syndrome and Casualties of War but Irreversible no.

Completely disagree. OP is asking for directors like Argento and De Palma, and both of them are well known for "shock value". Argento perhaps less so.

To be fair, I understand the point you're making, but we're talking an audience in 2024. Yes, the rape scene in Irreversible is confronting and uncomfortable, but from my perspective, isn't even on par with something like Possession (1981) even Martyrs (2008).

De Palme is well knwon for endangering women in his films, and Argento, it didn't really matter - whatever served the plot.

I think Noé does some absolutely ridiculous stuff with the female roles, and I admit that I'm not particularly a massive fan of what he does, but I also think his work absolutely needs to be seen.

Ti West does some remarkably fun and cool camerawork in Pearl and X. Definitely a lot of homages to De Palma visually and lots of bright and intense colors a la Argento. Also Chad Stahelski if you like John Wick doesn’t use his camera tne same as De Palma or Argento because of genre differences but I love the way the camera in his movies move around and he’s a master of bright flashing lights juxtaposed with darker shades for really exciting visual sets.

Mandy definitely feels reminiscent of Argento in the use of colours, music and violence (I haven’t seen the directors other films).

I also feel like Robert Eggers and Nicholas winding Refn are directors who have some of the same kind of stylisation.

There aren't a lot of direct modern parallels, kinky, violent, neo-Hitchcockian thrillers aren't really in vogue, but a few that come to mind:

Peter Strickland

David Robert Mitchell

Park Chan-wook

Thank you! Gasper Noe is a really good suggestion - I've seen Irreversible, but need to watch Enter the Void and Vortex (which I heard is great). Climax is also one that's been on my watchlist so long I forgot about it.

I've seen Irreversible, and thought the visual aspects were great and really interesting - but maybe the extreme nature of the story and violence distracted me from fully appreciating them or wanting to revisit it in the same way I would an Argento or De Palma film (ironically their films were also considered too violent in the 70's and 80's).

Argento and De Palma almost go for something melodramatic or heightened, making it feel a bit removed from reality - I'm aware of the camera moving, of the artifice of it all, and because of that I feel like I can think about the ideas in the film and appreciate the creativity a bit more clearly (If that makes sense?)

I would completely agree and think that Irreversible needs to be seen, but OP asked for recommendations along the lines of Body double, Dressed to kill, and Decision to leave. There is nothing in those movies that you couldn’t show to a 13 year old or even throw on at a party and nothing would be more than a slight shock. I just don’t think someone should potentially turn on Irreversible without realizing what they are in for.

Joe Begos has that color lighting in his works sans *Almost Human*. Though unlike DePalma and Argento, he doesn't owe much to Alfred Hitchcock, but rather genre cult filmmakers of the past like John Carpenter, Harry Bromley Davenport, and Gaspar Noe.

> [After fighting with censorship boards over the rating of Scarface — they rated it X and he had to battle to make it R — De Palma resolved to make Body Double as pushback. At the time, he said, "If this one doesn't get an X, nothing I ever do is going to. This is going to be the most erotic and surprising and thrilling movie I know how to make...I'm going to give them everything they hate and more of it than they've ever seen. They think Scarface was violent? They think my other movies were erotic? Wait until they see Body Double."](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_Double)
I wanna say I love Black Rainbow although it’s even lighter on plot than Mandy.

"kinky, violent, neo-Hitchcockian thrillers" is a good way to put it!

David Robert Mitchell is an interesting one. It Follows was definitely very John Carpenter influenced and has some excellent scenes. Under the Silver Lake is definitely more in the Hitchcock mystery vein. I remember watching it and feeling like it didn't do much for me at the time, but for some reason I still think about it every now and then as it had a really good sense of mystery - maybe it's time to revisit it!

Peter Stricklands films are definitely homages to Italian horror/giallos. I've liked them all, but I don't know if they go too far with the visual set-pieces and camera work like De Palma or Argento? It's been a while since I seen them though

I was gonna say Ti West also, as I heard his upcoming Maxxxine film is inspired by giallo films. Not sure if he’s shooting it on film (X was originally gonna be 16mm but Covid changed that), but I hope so.

Peter Strickland comes to mind. He directed Berbian Sound Studio… and it felt like it could exist among de Palma. 

It’s been a while since I’ve seen it but it came to my mind a few months back when I watched Blow Out.
Definitely Refn. His use of color, lighting and music..

I do too. I’m a huge horror fan in general, especially a lot of Giallo films so when I saw X for the first time I was immediately wowed and then with Pearl as one of the best prequels I’ve seen in a long time in or out of the horror genre I’m just ridiculously excited for Maxxxine. Ti West is gonna be an all time great horror director even if he stopped with this trilogy

I enjoyed X and Pearl a lot too, they were very well done. I remember X being more in the vein of Texas Chainsaw/Tobe Hooper, but now that you mention it, it did have that split screen scene which was a very De Palma-ish moment. Do you remember any other De Palma homages in there off the top of your head in there? Since Maxxxine is an 80's set sequel, fingers crossed he takes some more inspiration from Body Double or Dressed to Kill

If only people has some sort of resource. Say, and I'm just spitballing here, a vast web of interconnected computers where it was possible to search for things and discover more about them...

It is on you as a viewer to make informed decisions about what you watch.

I mean the relationship between Pearl and her mother was deeply reminiscent of that between Carrie and her mother, although that’s plot and not camera work. I’m not sure more about specifically camera work. I’d need to rewatch it again tbh.

Nicholas Winding Refn is a really good one, and someone who's maybe underappreciated for his strong visuals (imo!). Neon Demon is probably his most Argento inspired too. I've liked everything he's done (both film and series) and feel like with everything new he puts out he's going deeper into his own unique style - strong visuals, slow paced, immoral and detached characters, heavy primary colours etc. It's very cool to see.
That's true, it is reminiscent if Carrie! I think I'll give them a watch again soon, I haven't seen them since they came out

I don't know if anyone has mentioned these already, but writer/director team, Helene Cattet and Bruno Forzani, have done a couplathree Giallo riffs that I really enjoyed.

Amer[Amer](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1426352/?ref_=ext_shr) (2009)
The Strange Colour of Your Body's Tears[The Strange Colour of Your Body's Tears](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2733258/?ref_=ext_shr) (2013)
Let the Corpses Tan[Let the Corpses Tan](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt5827212/?ref_=ext_shr) (2017)

Amer is probably the one I like the most but all are worth a look if you're into extremely stylish, beautifully shot and fantastically scored genre flicks. Be warned though, they're low on plot and dialogue and more like sharply executed mood pieces that click all the better if you know what they're referencing. Definitely not for everyone. 

I'd liken them to visual albums that explore the imagery and tropes of Giallo to create something new. Maybe similar to how artists like Dilla or DJ Shadow recontextualised samples to build new tracks. The poster artwork, music, cinematography, editing and overall aesthetic are amazing. 

I sometimes part run and DJ occasional music nights that dip into soundtracks amongst other genres and we project these flicks in venues. People always ask what they are. Might be difficult to find on streaming services though and you'd have to maybe look into physical media. I have DVDs I bought when they came out.

I realise this might all sound dangerously artsy-fartsy and like pretentious hipster nonsense, but they're actually a lot of fun and know what they are. You'll either love them or hate them. No middle ground.

Park Chan-Wook is my personal recommendation as far as the evolution of these stylish plot (and cinematic emotion) driven filmmakers you've asked about. Decision to Leave was probably one of the most sober films that Brian De Palma never made.
Berberian Sound Studio and In Fabric definitely have that old school Italian giallo/horror vibe. The Duke of Burgundy is also great.
They’re both so good to do as a double feature. You notice so many little things that the two movies share.
Awesome, thanks for these! Low on plot mood pieces could describe for a lot of my favourite giallos too, so I'm looking forward to these

I agree with you.
It's wise, and in no way prudish, to warn people about Irreversible.

Irreversible is a wrecker. It's not comparable to DePalma or Argento, who despite their propensity towards violence and shock, create a deliberately stylised aesthetic and atmosphere that communicates "you're in a movie and so are they". Irreversible, despite its reversed structure and hyper-stylised aesthetic, throws the viewer right into the maelstrom of the violence. It will make you wince and feel terrible. As it should. It's definite nightmare material for some people. Especially today.

I grew up in the 80s and 90s and watched everything at a pretty young age (I'm much less inclined towards that kind of movie these days because I'm older and softer now), but I still recall seeing Irreversible and it being viscerally shocking. It's a great film that I personally felt I had no need to watch again. 

I'll probably get downvoted for this, but I'd be a little concerned about anyone who's watched it more than three times. There's nothing to reexamine. It's all there on the first watch. It does what it does, very successfully, and then it leaves to exist only in memory and pub conversations that go; "It's really good but I don't know if I'd really recommend watching it. It might not be for you." It's certainly not a rewatchable.
I looked him up, would Bliss be a good representation of his films?
yes. Absolutely.

No problem. 
It sounds like they'll be right up your street.
Hope you can find them. They've become cult favourites amongst my friends. 

I'd be intrigued to hear what you think once you've seen them.

Yes, I love his films! He's incredibly creative in how he visualises everything, from the camera movement to transitions. He seems to be always trying to find a great new way to show something .

How do you define the term "cinematic emotion"? (I think I know what you mean but I'm not fully sure)
Was going to say Mandy. Also the new [Rose Glass thing](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BF_J3-DmiS0) has some pretty stylized shots mixed in with the Adrian Lyne erotic thriller vibe.
[removed]

I've been re-watching my collection of De Palma films I have on physical disc. I don't have every single one but all of my favorites. (Which is most of them!) For my subjective perspective, "cinematic emotion" is how I would define those particular artists who are driven to use the precise language of the filmmaking to establish or heighten the emotional needs of a scene or a character. They are not complacent storytellers, using basic mise en scène to communicate. They are dynamic storytellers who are relying upon their editor(s), their cinematographer, their production design, their sound and music artists all in a tandem to accentuate the emotion. A lot of these filmmakers will often be chided by critics for relying on "substance over style" but in my opinion these are filmmakers who are using style to communicate beyond the substance visible in the script or simple performance. "Pure cinema," if you will. De Palma had it. Director Park also has it. In spades.
Refn has a very different style of editing though. His films feel much slower
[removed]
Seconding PCW. Decision to Leave is exactly what OP is looking for, and also one of the best films of the 2020s

It's delivered at a different pace but the guy you're looking for is Nicolas Winding Refn. 

NWR is our reigning Ero Art-Sleaze King and he is very consciously influenced by Arento who's extreme, expressionist style he takes and combines with the pacing inspired by slow cinema. It's not as apparent in his big hit Drive(2011) but its only gotten stronger as each subsequent work has only gotten more experimental--or as the haters might say, 'self-indulgent.'

For what you're asking for I can not recommend highly enough Refen's Netflix tv show from last year Copenhagen Cowboy. It's the story of a tracksuit wearing young witch's sojourn through the Danish criminal underworld where she does battle with a family of old money aristocratic vampires. All of the stylistic features you are describing are there; the suspense, the vivid use of colors, and extreme inventiveness with the camera. Refen is trying things with cameras in that show I've never seen before; in one extended scene he films a conversation between two characters in a room by putting the camera on a rotating stand and just letting it slowly pan around in circles while the characters are talking. 

I would describe myself as a Refen skeptic who hasn't like many of his movies but Copenhagen Cowboy won me over and from what you wrote it sounds exactly up your alley.
Love the Peter Strickland answer. He's got a little Argento, also has a little DePalma, and brings some of his own particular brand of crazy to the table.

Didn't even think of that, but Under the Silver Lake is so De Palma inspired. Guy tries to find out what happened to a pretty girl and, along the way, finds a whole other conspiracy. It's Def not a de palma specific story, but the way it's filmed and presented comes across as De Palma coded.
have you seen Too Old To Die Young? i wouldnt say im on the refn train, but im on the wagon for sure. I need to set some time aside for Copenhagen Cowboy.

Yes, I loved Copenhagen Cowboy too, and remember that exact shot you mentioned, it was really excellent. I enjoyed his previous series Too Old To Die Young too, but CC feels like an even more evolved and striking version of his style
Fair call! Can't disagree with anything you've said, but appreciate the back and forth in this thread. Thanks for engaging and showing me a different perspective, I appreciate it a lot!

This is a really really great definition, thank you for writing it! I'm really drawn to this style of dynamic filmmaking, and it's a shame it's not more common. I've seen Park Chan-wook say in an interview something similar to what you mentioned, how this style adds complexity and feeling to his film, and how he's always looking at how he can show something in a new way.

It's interesting that these filmmakers all work within suspense/thriller/horror genres. Possibly because the audiences are open to a more heightened experience in these genres? Or maybe it would just be strange to have some of these techniques in something like a straight drama (or even a rom-com), where you would maybe instead want the audience to forget about the camera and focus on the characters

In my opinion it is because those genres have the most use for cinematic language. They are essentially dreams or nightmares. It allows you to heighten the theatricality and embrace "opera," if you will.

Very "virtuoso" direction! It's typical of '70s. Similar to progressive rock in music! I love their style! Someone similar today? Nope, in contemporary directors you can find just the same or more intense adrenaline camera movements, unluckily not the same art and creativity. It isn't just a matter of technique. Today we have good directors too, but with different style and approach in different genres. See Robert Eggers, quite the opposite.
